part.title: First steps
part.description: Greetings, pronouns, the verb olla, saying no, asking questions and counting.

topics.title: Greetings & polite phrases
topics.summary: Hello, goodbye, how are you, thank you — and which greeting fits which time of day.

sections.heading: Hello & goodbye

rows: any time, informal (moi is very common)

sections.tip: **Hyvää** is the partitive of *hyvä* (good): greetings are short wishes — 'good day (to you)'.

rows: Hyvää, kiitos. Entä sinulle? — Fine, thanks. And you?
Hyvin! / Ihan hyvin. / Ei hassummin. / Huonosti.
Kuinka voit? — How are you feeling?
Here you are / You're welcome (sg. / pl. & polite)
Mikä sinun nimesi on? — Minun nimeni on …
What's your name? — My name is …
Mistä sinä olet kotoisin? — Olen kotoisin Englannista.
Where are you from? — I'm from England.

topics.title: Personal pronouns
topics.summary: minä, sinä, hän, me, te, he — and Finnish has no 'he' vs 'she'.

sections.heading: The six persons
bullets: **hän** covers both he and she — no grammatical gender anywhere in Finnish.
**te** is also the polite 'you' for one person (teititellä), e.g. with older strangers or in formal letters.
Because the verb ending shows the person, **minä, sinä, me, te are often dropped**: *(Minä) Asun Lontoossa.* — but **hän** and **he** are always kept.

sections.heading: Pronoun forms you will meet early

topics.title: The verb olla — to be
topics.summary: olen, olet, on, olemme, olette, ovat — the most important (and irregular) verb.

examples.en: I am Gavin. I am English.
He/she is a teacher.
We are at home.
You are Finnish (pl. → partitive plural).

examples.fi: Tämä on kirja. Kirja on punainen.
examples.en: This is a book. The book is red.
It is three o'clock.
Today is Monday.
It is cold outside (no 'it' in Finnish).

sections.heading: Good to know
bullets: There is **no word for 'a/an' or 'the'**: *Hän on opettaja* = he is a teacher.
With weather, time and temperature there is no subject: *On kylmä.* (It's cold.) *Sataa.* (It's raining.)
**olla + adessive** = to have: *Minulla on koira.* (see [[have-adessive|Minulla on]])
Spoken Finnish: mä oon, sä oot, se on, me ollaan, te ootte, ne on.

topics.title: Saying no: the negative verb
topics.summary: Finnish says 'no' with a verb of its own: en, et, ei, emme, ette, eivät + the verb's stem.

sections.heading: The negative verb changes, the main verb doesn't
sections.body: In a negative sentence the **person ending moves to the negative verb** *e-*, and the main verb loses its ending (it takes the same stem as the minä form, without -n).

sections.heading: How to make it
bullets: Take the **minä** form and remove **-n**: puhun → *puhu*, nukun → *nuku*, tapaan → *tapaa*.
Put the right form of **e-** in front: *en puhu, ei nuku, emme tapaa*.
Type 1 verbs with K-P-T keep the **weak** grade in all negative forms: *hän nukkuu* → *hän ei nuku* (see [[kpt-verbs|K-P-T in verbs]]).

sections.heading: Negation changes the object to partitive
sections.body: In a negative sentence the object (and the 'thing you have') goes into the **partitive**:

examples.fi: Minulla on auto. → Minulla ei ole autoa.
examples.en: I have a car. → I don't have a car.
I'll buy the book. → I won't buy a book.
He/she doesn't drink coffee.

sections.heading: Short answers

examples.en: Are you Finnish? — No (I'm not). / Yes (I am).
Do you speak Swedish? — No.

examples.fi: Asuuko hän Helsingissä? — Ei asu. / Asuu.
examples.en: Does he live in Helsinki? — No. / Yes.

sections.tip: Finns answer yes/no questions by **repeating the verb**: *Puhutko englantia? — Puhun.* A plain *kyllä/joo* or *ei* is also fine.

topics.title: Yes/no questions with -ko/-kö
topics.summary: Add -ko or -kö to the verb and move it to the front: Puhut suomea → Puhutko suomea?

sections.heading: How to build a yes/no question
bullets: Take the verb and add **-ko** (back-vowel words) or **-kö** (front-vowel words) — see [[vowel-harmony|vowel harmony]].
Put the verb **first** in the sentence.

sections.heading: Negative questions
sections.body: Add -kö to the negative verb (always -kö, because e- is a front word): **enkö, etkö, eikö, emmekö, ettekö, eivätkö**.

examples.en: Don't you speak Finnish?
Isn't he/she at home?

sections.heading: Focusing other words
sections.body: -ko/-kö can be attached to any word you want to question; that word goes first.

examples.en: Is it tomorrow that you're coming?
Is it coffee you're drinking?

topics.title: Question words
topics.summary: Mikä, kuka, missä, mistä, mihin, milloin, miten… Most question words are forms of mikä (what) and kuka (who).

rows: Mikä tämä on? — What is this?
Mitä sinä teet? — What are you doing?
Kuka hän on? — Who is he/she?
Kenen kirja tämä on? — Whose book is this?
Kenellä on avain? — Who has the key?
Missä sinä asut? — Where do you live?
Mistä sinä olet kotoisin? — Where are you from?
Mihin sinä menet? — Where are you going?
Milloin kurssi alkaa? — When does the course start?
Mitä kello on? / Paljonko kello on?
Miksi opiskelet suomea? — Why are you studying Finnish?
Paljonko tämä maksaa? — How much does this cost?
Millainen sää on tänään? — What's the weather like?

sections.heading: Missä — mistä — mihin
sections.body: The three 'where' words match the three directions of the [[local-cases|local cases]]. Always answer in the same direction:

examples.en: Where are you? — I'm in the shop.
Where are you coming from? — From the shop.
Where are you going? — To the shop.

sections.heading: Tip
sections.body: No -ko/-kö is added when the sentence already has a question word: *Missä sinä asut?* (not ✗*Missäkö*).

topics.title: Numbers
topics.summary: yksi, kaksi, kolme… Teens add -toista, tens add kymmentä, and the thing you count goes into the partitive.

sections.heading: Tens, hundreds, thousands
sections.body: Multiply with **kymmentä** (tens), **sataa** (hundreds), **tuhatta** (thousands) — these are partitive forms. Just write the parts one after the other (as one word up to 999).

sections.heading: Counting things: number + partitive
sections.body: After every number except *yksi* (1) the noun goes into the **partitive singular** — never plural.

examples.en: one cat — two cats
three children (lapsi → lasta)
five euros
twenty degrees

examples.fi: Minulla on kaksi veljeä ja yksi sisko.
examples.en: I have two brothers and one sister.

sections.heading: Ordinal numbers (1st, 2nd…)
sections.body: Used for dates and floors. Written with a full stop: 1. = ensimmäinen.

examples.en: I live on the third floor.

examples.fi: Paljonko tämä maksaa? — Se maksaa kolme euroa viisikymmentä (senttiä).
examples.en: How much is this? — It costs €3.50.

examples.fi: Puhelinnumeroni on nolla neljä nolla, yksi kaksi kolme…
examples.en: My phone number is 040 123… (digits one by one)

topics.title: Countries, nationalities & languages
topics.summary: Suomi → suomalainen → suomi (the language). Nationalities end in -lainen/-läinen; languages and nationalities are written with a small letter.

sections.heading: Rules
bullets: Nationality = country (or its stem) + **-lainen** (back words) / **-läinen** (front words): *Venäjä → venäläinen*.
Countries are capitalised; **nationalities and languages are not**: *Suomi* but *suomalainen*, *suomi*.
'I speak X' uses the **partitive**: *Puhun suomea, englantia ja vähän ruotsia.*
Plural of -nen words: *suomalainen → suomalaiset* (we are Finns: *Me olemme suomalaisia*).

examples.fi: Mistä sinä olet kotoisin? — Olen kotoisin Englannista.
examples.en: Where are you from? — I'm from England.

examples.fi: Hän on Ruotsista, mutta asuu Suomessa.
examples.en: He/she is from Sweden but lives in Finland.
